title: What is a foreign key, and what do `ON DELETE`/`ON UPDATE` clauses do?
shortTitle: What is a foreign key, and what do ON DELETE and ON UPDATE clauses do?

s1_definition.profdef: A foreign key is a column or set of columns in one table that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity so that a child row can only point at a parent row that actually exists. The `ON DELETE` and `ON UPDATE` clauses define what the database does to child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted or its key is updated, with options such as `RESTRICT`/`NO ACTION` (block it), `CASCADE` (propagate the delete or update to children), `SET NULL`, and `SET DEFAULT`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, every transaction belongs to an account. The account id stored on each transaction is a foreign key pointing back at the accounts table. The bank must never have a transaction pointing at an account that does not exist — that would be an orphan entry in the ledger. The `ON DELETE` rule decides what happens if someone tries to close Rajesh's account while transactions still reference it: block the closure, or automatically remove the transactions too, or leave the transactions but blank out the account link. The `ON UPDATE` rule does the same if the account id itself were changed.
s1_definition.oneliner: A foreign key makes a child row point only at an existing parent; `ON DELETE`/`ON UPDATE` decide whether removing or changing the parent is blocked, cascaded to children, or nulls the link.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A foreign key is a column or set of columns in one table that references the primary key of another table, enforcing referential integrity so that a child row can only point at a parent row that actually exists. The `ON DELETE` and `ON UPDATE` clauses define what the database does to child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted or its key is updated, with options such as `RESTRICT`/`NO ACTION` (block it), `CASCADE` (propagate the delete or update to children), `SET NULL`, and `SET DEFAULT`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, every transaction belongs to an account. The account id stored on each transaction is a foreign key pointing back at the accounts table. The bank must never have a transaction pointing at an account that does not exist — that would be an orphan entry in the ledger. The `ON DELETE` rule decides what happens if someone tries to close Rajesh's account while transactions still reference it: block the closure, or automatically remove the transactions too, or leave the transactions but blank out the account link. The `ON UPDATE` rule does the same if the account id itself were changed.

**One line to remember:** A foreign key makes a child row point only at an existing parent; `ON DELETE`/`ON UPDATE` decide whether removing or changing the parent is blocked, cascaded to children, or nulls the link.

sections.s2_technical:
A foreign key is a constraint, not just a column. You declare it with `REFERENCES parent(column)`, and from that moment the database guarantees that every value in the foreign-key column either matches an existing value in the referenced parent column or is null. This is referential integrity: it prevents orphan rows, such as a transaction whose account was never created or was deleted out from under it. Because the foreign key references a key that must be unique, it almost always points at the parent's primary key or a unique constraint.

The interesting behavior is what happens when the parent changes. By default most databases use `RESTRICT` or `NO ACTION`, which means the database blocks any attempt to delete or change a parent row that still has children, forcing you to deal with the children first. `ON DELETE CASCADE` means deleting the parent automatically deletes all its child rows in the same transaction — useful when children have no meaning without the parent, such as deleting an order and all its line items together. `ON DELETE SET NULL` means the child rows survive but their foreign-key column is set to null, severing the link while keeping the record — appropriate when a child can meaningfully exist without a parent, such as keeping an audit log entry even after the related account is gone. `ON DELETE SET DEFAULT` sets the column to its declared default instead of null. The `ON UPDATE` clause mirrors these: `ON UPDATE CASCADE` propagates a change in the parent key down to all children so the references stay valid, which is one way people cope when a natural primary key changes, though it is exactly the pain a surrogate key avoids.

Choosing the right action is a design decision with real consequences. `CASCADE` on delete is powerful but dangerous: a single delete at the top of a hierarchy can silently remove enormous amounts of data, so in financial systems teams often prefer `RESTRICT` and explicit, audited deletions, or soft deletes that flag a row as inactive rather than removing it. A senior nuance is performance and locking: cascading operations can touch many rows and hold locks, and foreign keys add a check on every insert and update, so very high-write systems sometimes enforce integrity in the application layer, though that trades safety for speed and is controversial. Another nuance is that the foreign-key column should be indexed, because without an index the database may scan the child table to check for referencing rows on parent deletes, and because foreign-key joins are common. In a banking ledger, the usual choice is `RESTRICT` on accounts so you cannot delete an account with transactions, combined with soft deletes, so history is never silently destroyed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must guarantee that every transaction references a real account. Early on, a bug inserted transactions with a mistyped account id, creating orphan ledger entries that nobody could trace. This is exactly what a foreign key prevents by rejecting any transaction whose account id does not exist.

Problem 2 — When a customer requests account closure, the bank must not silently erase their transaction history, because regulators require it to be retained. So deleting an account that still has transactions must be blocked. This is exactly `ON DELETE RESTRICT`. For a different table, customer notification preferences, it is fine to cascade-delete when the customer is removed, so that table uses `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

The mini-project creates accounts and transactions with a `RESTRICT` foreign key and a preferences table with a `CASCADE` foreign key, then a demo that shows an orphan transaction is rejected, deleting an account with transactions is blocked, and deleting a customer cascades to their preferences.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id          VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00
);

CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(24) PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    -- FK with RESTRICT: cannot delete an account that still has transactions.
    CONSTRAINT fk_txn_account FOREIGN KEY (account_id)
        REFERENCES accounts(id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT
        ON UPDATE CASCADE          -- if id ever changes, propagate to keep links valid
);
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id);  -- index the FK column

CREATE TABLE notification_prefs (
    id          BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    channel     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,  -- SMS, EMAIL, PUSH
    -- FK with CASCADE: deleting the account removes its preferences automatically.
    CONSTRAINT fk_pref_account FOREIGN KEY (account_id)
        REFERENCES accounts(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, holder_name, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 'Rajesh Kumar', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001', 'Priya Sharma', 250000.00);
INSERT INTO transactions (txn_id, account_id, amount) VALUES
    ('TXN-0001', 'SAV2001', 50000.00);
INSERT INTO notification_prefs (account_id, channel) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 'SMS'), ('SAV2001', 'EMAIL');
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: accounts SAV2001 (with one transaction and two notification preferences) and CUR3001 (with neither), then three operations.

Step 1: The first operation inserts a transaction for account ZZZ9999, which does not exist. The foreign key checks the accounts table, finds no matching parent, and rejects the insert as a foreign-key violation. No orphan is created.

Step 2: The second operation tries to delete account SAV2001, which still has transaction TXN-0001. The `ON DELETE RESTRICT` rule blocks the delete, so the account and its history are preserved. The database raises a foreign-key violation and nothing is removed.

Step 3: The third operation deletes account CUR3001, which has no transactions, so `RESTRICT` does not block it. The delete succeeds. Because any notification preferences for CUR3001 used `ON DELETE CASCADE`, they would be removed automatically in the same transaction.

Step 4: The end state shows SAV2001 and its history intact, CUR3001 gone along with its dependent preferences, and no orphan transactions anywhere.

```text
Feb 14,2026 11:05:00 SEVERE LedgerDao - Rejected TXN-9999: insert or update on table "transactions" violates foreign key constraint "fk_txn_account"
Feb 14,2026 11:05:00 SEVERE LedgerDao - Cannot delete SAV2001: update or delete on table "accounts" violates foreign key constraint "fk_txn_account" on table "transactions"
Feb 14,2026 11:05:00 INFO  LedgerDao - Deleted account CUR3001
Feb 14,2026 11:05:00 INFO  ForeignKeyDemo - FK blocks orphans; RESTRICT protects history; CASCADE cleans dependents.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  accounts (parent)                 transactions (child)
    id = SAV2001  ◀──── FK account_id ──── TXN-0001
    id = CUR3001                            (ON DELETE RESTRICT, ON UPDATE CASCADE)

  op1: INSERT txn account_id=ZZZ9999 → no parent → FK VIOLATION → REJECT
  op2: DELETE account SAV2001 (has txn) → RESTRICT → BLOCKED
  op3: DELETE account CUR3001 (no txn) → allowed
        └─ notification_prefs (ON DELETE CASCADE) → its pref rows auto-deleted
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Foreign Key Actions ═══

  ┌─ ON DELETE / ON UPDATE options ──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ RESTRICT/NO ACTION: block if children exist (safe default)       │
  │ CASCADE:            propagate delete/update to children          │
  │ SET NULL:           keep child, null the FK link                 │
  │ SET DEFAULT:        set FK to its column default                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ Design choices (banking) ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ accounts←transactions : RESTRICT  (never silently lose ledger)   │
  │ accounts←prefs        : CASCADE   (dependents, safe to clean up) │
  │ index the FK column   : fast joins + fast parent-delete checks   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Entity Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────┐ 1   * ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ accounts             │◆─────→│ transactions             │
  │ + id PK              │ RESTRICT │ account_id FK           │
  └──────────┬───────────┘       └──────────────────────────┘
             │ 1   *  CASCADE
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ notification_prefs       │
  │ account_id FK            │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  Contract for deleteAccount():
    Pre:  account may or may not have children
    Post: deleted IFF no RESTRICT child; CASCADE children auto-removed
    Throws: FK violation if RESTRICT child exists
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A foreign key is a constraint that makes a column in one table reference the primary key of another table, so the database guarantees every child value either matches an existing parent row or is null. That is referential integrity, and its job is to prevent orphan rows — a transaction pointing at an account that never existed or was deleted out from under it. Because it references a key that must be unique, a foreign key almost always points at the parent's primary key.

The `ON DELETE` and `ON UPDATE` clauses define what happens when the referenced parent is deleted or its key changes. The default is usually `RESTRICT` or `NO ACTION`, which blocks the operation while children still exist. `CASCADE` propagates the delete or update to the children, so deleting a parent deletes all its children in the same transaction. `SET NULL` keeps the children but severs the link by nulling the foreign-key column, and `SET DEFAULT` sets it to the column's default. On update, `CASCADE` propagates a changed parent key down so references stay valid, which is one way to cope when a natural key changes, and is exactly the pain a surrogate key avoids.

Choosing the action is a real design decision. Cascading deletes are powerful but dangerous because one delete at the top of a hierarchy can silently wipe out huge amounts of data, so in financial systems we usually prefer `RESTRICT` plus soft deletes so history is never silently destroyed. The senior points are to index the foreign-key column because otherwise parent deletes and joins can scan the child table, and that foreign keys add a check on every write, which very high-write systems occasionally move to the application layer at the cost of safety. At the National Bank of India our transactions reference accounts with `ON DELETE RESTRICT` so you cannot close an account that still has ledger history, while notification preferences reference accounts with `ON DELETE CASCADE` because they are meaningless once the account is gone. The line I always state is that a foreign key makes a child point only at an existing parent, and `ON DELETE` and `ON UPDATE` decide whether touching the parent is blocked, cascaded, or nulls the link.
